communication_expectations: Camden is 4 years old and his MOTHER is the respondent for this interview: she answers every question about him as his primary caregiver/historian (the transcript labels her responses 'PATIENT (Camden's Mother)'). The student is still assessing Camden as the patient. Warm, family-centered communication is expected; the student may address Camden and/or his mother, and adult medical jargon is inappropriate. Engaging Camden's interests (exploring, shows, his goldfish Turbo, stuffed animals) is a strength. Do NOT penalize the student because Camden himself is not speaking - the caregiver being the historian is expected and age-appropriate.
caregiver_rules: The mother is the speaking respondent and answers on Camden's behalf. Caregiver-directed or caregiver-referenced questioning is expected and age-appropriate. The student should not be penalized for gathering history via the caregiver, nor for the fact that the 4-year-old does not self-report clinical detail.
patient_goals: Play outside again and go 'exploring' in parks

assessment_areas.assessment_area: understanding of condition and treatment experience
assessment_areas.case_context: Camden is 3 months into treatment for high-risk acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The student should gently explore how treatment is going in child-appropriate terms (medicine, feeling sick, tired days).
acceptable_approaches: child-framed questions about medicine and feeling sick
caregiver-referenced questions
following up on what Camden volunteers

assessment_areas.case_context: Camden has documented bone pain (7/10), muscle aches (4/10), and tingling in hands and feet. Child-appropriate pain exploration (where it hurts, when, what makes it better) is expected.
acceptable_approaches: simple 'owie' language and body-part questions
asking about pain during specific activities like stairs or play
faces-scale style questions

assessment_areas.case_context: He tires quickly; intense activity provokes pain, and he can no longer keep up with his brother.
acceptable_approaches: asking about play and tired feelings
asking what he can and cannot do now versus before

assessment_areas.case_context: Functional changes include impaired running and crawling, weaker grip (crayons, buttons, pouring milk), and staying inside watching TV instead of exploring outdoors.
acceptable_approaches: asking about favorite play and what changed
asking about hands and drawing
asking about keeping up with his brother

assessment_areas.case_context: The family is managing the emotional impact of the diagnosis; he lives with his mom and brother, and his grandmother homeschools the boys.
acceptable_approaches: gentle questions about home and family
responding to emotional cues with warmth
caregiver-context questions

assessment_areas.case_context: His appetite is different and eating is harder since treatment; his tummy sometimes feels bad after medicine.
acceptable_approaches: simple food questions
asking about tummy feelings after medicine

assessment_areas.case_context: Rest is a documented part of his routine; sleep totals are otherwise unremarkable in the record.
acceptable_approaches: asking about naps, rest, and bedtime in child terms

assessment_areas.case_context: Camden is receiving chemotherapy (vincristine, dexamethasone). Age-appropriate screening for feeling sick, fevers, or new symptoms - or caregiver-directed screening - is a relevant safety behavior; his hand/foot tingling (possible treatment-related neuropathy) also deserves follow-up if disclosed.
acceptable_approaches: asking if he has felt hot, sick, or has new owies
caregiver-framed screening
following up on tingling or numb feelings

assessment_areas.assessment_area: adult lifestyle screening (work, substances, adult exercise programming)
assessment_areas.case_context: Adult-oriented screening topics are not appropriate for a 4-year-old and must not be expected.
